A sparse random projection for forest initialization

Source: vignettes/articles/sparse-rp-example.Rmd
sparse-rp-example.Rmd

Fair warning, this article ends in defeat. But I had the idea, and I tried the idea, and I am now writing this down so I don’t forget and try it again another day.

The tree-count article explores the trade-off between forest time and recall. High-dimensional data takes a noticeably longer amount of time to build and at least at low k, recall from a forest can be underwhelming, although it is better than initializing nearest neighbor descent with the projected data than using random initialization.

So could we make the forest cheaper by pre-processing the input data to a lower dimensional space? PCA is the obvious choice, but even approaches based on truncated SVD (like irlba) can be slower than building the forest in the original space. A much faster approach is to use random projections.

The intriguing idea originating with Johnson and Lindenstrauss (1984) is that a random projection into a lower dimensional space approximately preserves pairwise distances, depending on the number of dimensions. This projection can be done very quickly and further work by Achlioptas (2003) shows you can do the projection with a matrix containing only +1, -1 and 0 as entries. Even better, Li, Hastie and Church (2006) show you can make this matrix very sparse, so storing the projection matrix can be very cheap.

In this article, we use a very sparse random projection (SRP) to map the whole dataset down to 128 dimensions, then build an ordinary random projection forest on the projected data. This global projection is separate from the randomized splits made at individual tree nodes. As you will see the results are probably not worth the extra effort of implementation, mainly that it’s an extra complication in the projection forest storage. And technically this only makes sense for Euclidean distances, so this would be a lot of extra machinery that only works for one metric (albeit a very common one).

Data and setup

The comparisons use macosko2015 mouse retina single-cell RNA sequencing data (3,000 gene expression features), MNIST handwritten digits, and COIL20 object images.

Dataset Observations Features
macosko2015 44,808 3,000
MNIST 70,000 784
COIL20 1,440 16,384
Gaussian 10,000 1,000

For the recipe, use the 1,000-dimensional independent standard normal Gaussian data from the tree-count article, a difficult neighbor-search example; X contains all reference rows, and separately generated query rows Q represent future observations with the same features in the same order.

library(rnndescent)
library(Matrix)
set.seed(20261105)
X <- matrix(rnorm(10000 * 1000), nrow = 10000)
set.seed(907)
Q <- matrix(rnorm(256 * 1000), nrow = 256)
k <- 15L
build_k <- k + 1L # Allow for self in the reference graph.
threads <- 8L

Project and build

Pass candidate indices alone so that rnnd_build() calculates Euclidean distances using the original features.

Following Li, Hastie and Church (2006), the map uses nonzero probability \rho = 1/\sqrt{d}, equally likely positive and negative (Rademacher) signs, and scale 1/\sqrt{m\rho}, where d is the original feature count and m the projected feature count.

sparse_sign_map <- function(d, m) {
  rho <- 1 / sqrt(d)
  Matrix::rsparsematrix(
    d,
    m,
    nnz = rbinom(1, d * m, rho),
    rand.x = function(n) sample(c(-1, 1), n, replace = TRUE) / sqrt(m * rho)
  )
}
set.seed(42)
P <- sparse_sign_map(ncol(X), 128L)
Z <- as.matrix(X %*% P)
rp <- rpf_knn(
  Z,
  k = build_k,
  include_self = FALSE,
  ret_forest = TRUE,
  n_threads = threads
)
index <- rnnd_build(
  X,
  k = build_k,
  metric = "euclidean",
  init = rp$idx,
  n_threads = threads
)
forest <- rpf_filter(
  nn = index$graph,
  forest = rp$forest,
  n_trees = 1L,
  n_threads = threads
)
model <- list(
  index = index,
  map = P,
  forest = forest
)
saveRDS(model, "sparse-rp-index.rds")

Query

Because querying only uses one tree, the effect of the sparse projection is minimized, so I won’t present any results for query performance in this article, but the code is here for completeness.

model <- readRDS("sparse-rp-index.rds")
Z <- as.matrix(crossprod(model$index$data, model$map))
Zq <- as.matrix(Q %*% model$map)
starts <- rpf_knn_query(
  Zq,
  Z,
  model$forest,
  k = k,
  n_threads = threads
)
neighbors <- rnnd_query(
  model$index,
  Q,
  k = k,
  init = starts$idx,
  n_threads = threads
)
head(cbind(row_in_X = neighbors$idx[1, ], distance = neighbors$dist[1, ]))

A small comparison

These benchmarks used rnndescent at commit f648624c, before later changes to forest construction and distance calculations. Timings and recall may differ with the current implementation.

The comparisons use Euclidean distance and eight threads. Build times are medians over five seeds and include index preparation, but exclude serialization. The recall column compares nonself neighbors with saved reference neighbors calculated from brute force search.

At k = 15:

Dataset Forest Build median (s) Graph recall (%)
macosko2015 Ordinary, 20 trees 63.05 46.50
macosko2015 Ordinary, 5 trees 47.64 43.10
macosko2015 Projected, 20 trees 38.51 43.46
MNIST Ordinary, 21 trees 12.42 98.86
MNIST Ordinary, 5 trees 11.76 98.57
MNIST Projected, 21 trees 7.50 98.62
Gaussian Ordinary, 15 trees 2.66 38.01
Gaussian Ordinary, 5 trees 2.33 36.71
Gaussian Projected, 15 trees 2.27 37.23
COIL20 Ordinary, 11 trees 2.61 99.95
COIL20 Ordinary, 5 trees 2.09 99.90
COIL20 Projected, 11 trees 1.64 99.94

Using the SRP data, the build time is even faster than a 5-tree forest in the original space. But recall is only slightly higher than that 5-tree forest. So you could argue that instead of using SRP, you should just use a 5-tree forest in the original space and save yourself the hassle of managing the sparse projection matrix.

Saved index size and projection regeneration

Is there any advantage in index size at least? We are only having to save 128 dimensions to define the split at each node of the trees, compared to 3,000 for e.g. macosko2015, and the only extra cost is the storage of the sparse signed projection matrix. Its nonzero entries have equal magnitude, so it should be very efficient to store.

At k = 15, these are the median gzip-compressed RDS sizes in MiB for complete models:

Dataset Ordinary, default trees Ordinary, 5 trees Projected, default trees Regenerate Z (s)
macosko2015 38.74 38.65 31.38 0.253
MNIST 39.65 39.64 39.14 0.143
Gaussian 80.87 80.76 75.90 0.014
COIL20 24.88 24.89 20.62 0.019

The SRP models are smaller, but the original reference data and the neighbor and search graphs still need to be saved. Both methods retain only one query tree, so reducing the number of trees used during construction barely changes the saved size.

Because we don’t save the Z matrix, it needs to be regenerated. The regeneration column shows how much time that takes (again a median of 5 runs just to be consistent). It is not a major bottleneck.

Building 50 neighbors

Dataset Forest Build median (s) Graph recall (%)
macosko2015 Ordinary, 20 trees 173.90 77.972
macosko2015 Ordinary, 5 trees 177.85 76.798
macosko2015 Projected, 20 trees 164.28 77.202
MNIST Ordinary, 21 trees 42.29 99.933
MNIST Ordinary, 5 trees 48.83 99.921
MNIST Projected, 21 trees 40.92 99.924
Gaussian Ordinary, 15 trees 10.83 83.387
Gaussian Ordinary, 5 trees 11.01 83.165
Gaussian Projected, 15 trees 11.08 84.656
COIL20 Ordinary, 11 trees 12.48 99.994
COIL20 Ordinary, 5 trees 13.10 99.983
COIL20 Projected, 11 trees 12.43 99.996

If we go up to 50 nearest neighbors, then using n_trees = 5 is slower than using the default larger number of trees. This is because the NND from a worse initialization spends more time optimizing. For a fixed number of trees, the time taken is not hugely affected and neither is recall: sometimes a bit better, sometimes a bit worse.

What if descent also uses the projection?

One last idea: it would at least be a bit less awkward to use SRP if it was a preprocessing step: do the projection once and then do the nearest neighbor search on that projected data, i.e. the RP forest and then nearest neighbor descent. If you wanted the distances in the original space, you can just calculate that at the end using the returned indices. The recall goes down a bit in the tree-building step, but maybe NND can recover it, and the distance calculation will be faster, so it might be worth a try?

For example, build the graph on Z, then rescore its nonself neighbors on X and order them by their original-space distances.

set.seed(42)
projected_index <- rnnd_build(
  Z,
  k = build_k,
  metric = "euclidean",
  init = "tree",
  n_trees = 15L,
  leaf_size = build_k,
  n_search_trees = 1L,
  n_threads = threads
)
ids <- remove_self_knn(projected_index$graph, k = k)$idx
original_neighbors <- sort_knn(
  knn_distances(X, ids, metric = "euclidean", n_threads = threads)
)
Dataset k Projected forest only: s / recall (%) Projected forest and descent: s / recall (%)
macosko2015 15 38.51 / 43.456 4.38 / 7.791
macosko2015 50 164.28 / 77.202 11.98 / 11.050
MNIST 15 7.50 / 98.618 4.22 / 65.194
MNIST 50 40.92 / 99.924 13.37 / 67.690
Gaussian 15 2.27 / 37.229 0.56 / 1.774
Gaussian 50 11.08 / 84.656 1.82 / 4.030
COIL20 15 1.64 / 99.940 0.28 / 86.528
COIL20 50 12.43 / 99.996 0.59 / 83.332

Oh dear. It’s certainly much faster (and that includes recalculating the distances in the original space and sorting them), but the recall is a bit of a disaster in all cases.

So for high-dimensional data and a small number of neighbors, there might be an interesting idea lurking in here somewhere. Maybe using more than 128 dimensions would help? But I am not inclined to explore that further.

References

  • Johnson, W. B. and Lindenstrauss, J. (1984). Extensions of Lipschitz mappings into a Hilbert space. Contemporary Mathematics, 26, 189–206. PDF
  • Achlioptas, D. (2003). Database-friendly random projections: Johnson-Lindenstrauss with binary coins. Journal of Computer and System Sciences, 66(4), 671–687. PDF
  • Li, P., Hastie, T. J. and Church, K. W. (2006). Very sparse random projections. Proceedings of KDD ’06, 287–296. PDF
